title: Microbatch stream demux and KV staleness handbook
content:
Summary:

This note documents a pragmatic approach to interleaving prefill and decode work in the serving runtime with two primary objectives: (1) preserve low tail latency for interactive decode streams, and (2) maximize GPU utilization through coalesced microbatches and KV cache reuse. The emphasis is on an operationally simple scheduler that reduces priority inversion and controls KV staleness without requiring global synchronization barriers.

Problem statement / motivation:

We observe three recurring tensions in production workloads:

1) Prefill-heavy batches (long context, few concurrent decodes) are efficient for kernel throughput but can block low-latency interactive decodes when we eagerly allocate slots for large prefill microbatches.

2) Decode streaming requests (short token emission) need rapid forward passes and KV cache access. When KV is evicted/recomputed too often (or becomes stale relative to a prefill), decode quality or throughput suffers.

3) Simple FIFO or pure batch-coalescing heuristics maximize throughput but cause tail-latency spikes for interactive traffic and can starve high-priority customers.

Design goals (ranked):

- P1: Per-stream decode tail latency <= configured SLO (e.g., 95th percentile < X ms)
- P2: Maintain high GPU utilization by enabling microbatch coalescing across streams where latency budget permits
- P3: Bound KV staleness (number of token-steps between prefill and subsequent decode using same cache) to avoid quality regressions and excessive recomputation
- P4: Operational simplicity and debuggability; minimize global locking and avoid full-epoch KV syncs

Key concepts introduced here:

- Stream Watermark: a per-stream logical timestamp representing the highest absolute token index that has been materialized into KV for that stream. Watermarks move forward on prefill completion and on decode epoch completion where applicable.

- Staleness Budget: a configurable integer (tokens) per model/profile determining the maximum acceptable difference between stream watermark and the token index required by an incoming decode. If decode requires tokens beyond watermark+budget then a local prefill must be scheduled (or we fall back to slower recompute).
- Demux Windows: short scheduling time-slices (e.g., 1–3ms) during which the scheduler collects arrivals and forms candidate microbatches. Windows are microsecond-granular buckets used for coalescing without imposing long queuing delays.

- Credit-Weighted Priority: each stream has credits derived from service tier / explicit priority; credits decay over time. Credits determine ordering when competing for a demux window. This prevents starvation while allowing throughput hunting when credits low.

High-level scheduling loop (per-GPU worker):

1) Arrival queue accepts prefill and decode requests. Each arrival annotated with stream_id, token-range (start,end), priority, and requested latency budget.

2) On each demux window tick: sample head of arrival queue for up to W ms window. Partition requests into two logical buckets: latency-sensitive (decode with tight budget) and throughput-friendly (prefill or decode with loose budget).

3) For latency-sensitive bucket: form microbatches bounded by max_decode_batch_size and prioritized by credit-weighted earliest-deadline. Flush those microbatches immediately (no wait beyond the window).

4) For throughput-friendly bucket: attempt cross-stream coalescing with heuristic: prefer batches that share model and comparable sequence length and that do not cause watermark staleness > staleness_budget for any included stream. If a stream would exceed staleness budget by joining, drop it from coalescing and schedule a local serialized prefill instead.

5) KV cache policy: for coalesced prefill, write through the KV store and advance stream watermark atomically at microbatch completion. For serialized small prefill done to satisfy a decode, we may write a lightweight delta cache and mark watermark as tentative until commit to persistent KV slot (optimizes lock hold time).

KV staleness handling and heuristics:

- Proactive refresh: for streams that see frequent decodes immediately after prefill (pattern detection), pre-schedule a lightweight short prefill to extend KV beyond current watermark when GPU idle cycles are >20% for a sliding window.

- Opportunistic compaction: if a stream’s KV grows large but is rarely read, a background compaction job can snapshot recent prefix and expire older layers; this is orthogonal but reduces memory pressure that causes forced eviction and recompute storms.

- Read-before-write check: when a decode arrives requiring tokens overlapping or beyond watermark, first check whether the missing portion can be patched via a delta prefill (short prefix) vs a full recompute. Use measured kernel cost model to pick path with lowest expected latency.

Priority inversion safeguards:

We ran into priority inversion when long prefill microbatches always absorbed the demux window. To mitigate: implement two levers in the scheduler:

A) Guaranteed fast-lane capacity: reserve N tokens-worth of GPU slots per worker for latency-sensitive decodes. These are priced out of throughput coalescing and cannot be consumed by throughput work unless left idle for T_idle ms.

B) Preemption boundary: microbatches longer than X tokens are checkpointed into sub-batches at the kernel boundary. The worker may preempt remaining sub-batches if a high-priority decode arrives; the partially executed work leaves a consistent KV to resume. This requires kernels to support mid-microbatch checkpointing (we map to per-layer host staging points).

Kernel & execution considerations:

- Kernel Affinity: prefer assembling coalesced microbatches with matching sequence-length buckets to avoid drifting into slow kernels. Maintain fast-path for mixed-length microbatches only if the length variance <= 2x and expected wasted compute < threshold.

- KV-locality hints: attach a small bitmap to each stream slot indicating last-compiled kernel variant and quantization path. Scheduler prefers grouping streams with matching KV-locality to reuse warmed device pages and reduce JIT overhead.

- Continuous batching implication on memory: when coalescing, peak memory can spike. Use a conservative packing algorithm that simulates per-stream KV footprints and rejects coalesces that would push over memory pressure thresholds. This is cheaper than speculative OOM and avoids eviction thrash.

Operational signals and metrics to surface:

- Per-stream watermark lag distribution: histogram of (required_token_index - watermark) for served decodes. Significant right tail -> prefill too stale.
- Microbatch coalesce ratio: (tokens served via coalesced vs serialized prefill). Trend up during off-peak is good.
- Fast-lane utilization: percent of reserved low-latency slots in use. Low utilization with elevated tail-latency indicates misclassification of workloads.
- Preemption events/time saved: count how often preemption invoked and aggregate latency improvement per event.

Fallback and incompatibility modes:

- If a model/kernel lacks preemption-friendly checkpointing, fall back to simpler fast-lane reservation and reduce long-microbatch size cap.
- For privacy-sensitive private deployments where KV must be strict, allow customers to disable cross-stream coalescing (explicit flag) and instead prefer per-tenant isolation; this accepts throughput loss for stronger isolation.

Open questions / trade-offs we are still weighing:

1) Watermark semantics for multi-tenant streams that share prefix history across requests: should watermark be per-(stream,tenant) or per-(logical-session)? Centralizing reduces storage but complicates correctness.

2) How aggressive should proactive refresh be? Too aggressive wastes cycles; too conservative causes staleness. We think an RL-based policy could adapt but initial implementation should be simple threshold-based with offline tuning.

3) Complexity vs. benefit for mid-microbatch checkpoints: kernel changes are non-trivial; are the latency gains worth the engineering cost? Short-term: emulate preemption by splitting big microbatches at compile-time rather than true runtime checkpointing.

Implementation plan (phases):

Phase 0 (experiment): add demux-window collector and fast-lane reservation in worker loop. Implement watermarks as in-memory monotonic counters. No kernel changes. Instruments metrics above.

Phase 1 (heuristics): add staleness budget checks, opportunistic compaction flag, and simple packing mem-simulation to coalesce safe microbatches. Add per-stream crediting.

Phase 2 (performance): introduce kernel affinity hints (compile-time annotations), small support for delta-prefills (very short prefix kernels), and simulated preemption via microbatch splitting.

Phase 3 (optional/longer term): real mid-microbatch checkpointing support in kernels and adaptive proactive refresh via an online learner.

Immediate TODOs (owners):

- Maya: prototype demux-window collector + metrics (2w).
- Leo: implement watermark counters and staleness-budget enforcement in scheduler (2w).
- Ivy: run offline traces to compute recommended default staleness budgets per model size (3w).
- Rohan: PR for fast-lane reservation and microbatch-splitting heuristics (3w).

Notes to reviewers:

- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: prioritize low-latency correctness first, then throughput improvements that do not increase operator cognitive load.
- Look at INF-2345 for trace examples (embedded tail-latency traces) and PR #789 for prior microbatching attempts that caused inversion.

Appendix (examples):

Example 1: Interactive chat stream (high priority) concurrently with a large offline summarization prefill. Demux window isolates the chat decode into fast-lane and coalesces the summarization with other throughput jobs. Watermark ensures the chat decode uses an up-to-date KV; if not, a quick delta-pre-fill is scheduled and executed in the fast-lane.

Example 2: Many small decodes hitting same conversation context. Instead of recomputing full prefill per decode, use a shared KV slot per-session; demux merges close temporal arrivals into a single prefill then fans out decodes. Staleness budget prevents over-sharing when edits occur.

End.
